questions.q: Print the directory you are currently in.
questions.explain: `pwd` prints the absolute path of the current directory.

questions.q: List ALL files (including hidden dotfiles) in long format.
questions.output:
total 32
drwxr-xr-x 4 user user 4096 Nov 23 09:12 .
drwxr-xr-x 3 root root 4096 Nov  1 08:00 ..
-rw------- 1 user user  812 Nov 23 09:10 .bash_history
-rw-r--r-- 1 user user 3771 Nov  1 08:00 .bashrc
drwxr-xr-x 2 user user 4096 Nov 20 14:02 scripts
questions.explain: `-l` = long listing (permissions, owner, size, date), `-a` = include hidden files that start with a dot.

questions.q: Change into the /etc directory.
questions.explain: `cd /etc`. `cd ..` goes up a level, `cd ~` (or just `cd`) goes home, `cd -` goes back to the previous directory.

questions.q: Create a new directory called backups.
questions.explain: `mkdir backups`. Add `-p` to create nested parents in one go: `mkdir -p backups/2026/11`.

questions.q: Make the file deploy.sh executable.
questions.explain: `chmod +x deploy.sh` adds execute permission. Then run it with `./deploy.sh`. Octal `chmod 755` also works (rwxr-xr-x).

questions.q: Print the contents of the file /etc/hostname to the screen.
questions.explain: `cat` prints a file. For long files use `less` (scrollable), `head` (first 10 lines) or `tail` (last 10).

questions.q: Show only the lines containing the word error in app.log.
questions.output:
2026-11-23 09:14:02 error: upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out)
2026-11-23 09:20:47 error: connect() failed (111: Connection refused)
questions.explain: `grep pattern file` prints matching lines. Useful flags: `-i` ignore case, `-n` line numbers, `-v` invert, `-r` recursive, `-c` count.

questions.q: Count the number of LINES in access.log.
questions.explain: `wc -l` counts lines (`-w` words, `-c` bytes). Combine with grep: `grep 404 access.log | wc -l`, or simply `grep -c 404 access.log`.

questions.q: Watch /var/log/syslog live as new lines are written.
questions.output:
Nov 23 09:31:12 netrealm-srv01 sshd[2211]: Accepted publickey for user from 10.0.0.8
Nov 23 09:31:14 netrealm-srv01 systemd[1]: Started Session 42 of user user.
questions.explain: `tail -f` follows the file as it grows. Press Ctrl+C to stop. On systemd hosts `journalctl -f` does the same for the journal.

questions.q: Show the IP addresses assigned to this machine's interfaces (modern iproute2 way).
questions.output:
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP> mtu 65536
    inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
2: eth0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP> mtu 1500
    inet 10.0.0.21/24 brd 10.0.0.255 scope global eth0
questions.explain: `ip a` (short for `ip address show`) replaces the deprecated `ifconfig`.

questions.q: Display this host's routing table.
questions.output:
default via 10.0.0.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100
10.0.0.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 10.0.0.21
questions.explain: `ip route` shows routes; 'default via 10.0.0.1' is the default gateway. Older equivalents: `route -n`, `netstat -rn`.

questions.q: List all listening TCP and UDP ports, numerically, with the owning process.
questions.output:
Netid State  Local Address:Port  Process
udp   UNCONN 0.0.0.0:68           users:(("dhclient",pid=612))
tcp   LISTEN 0.0.0.0:22           users:(("sshd",pid=801))
tcp   LISTEN 0.0.0.0:443          users:(("nginx",pid=1123))
questions.explain: `ss -tulpn`: t=TCP, u=UDP, l=listening, p=process, n=numeric. It answers 'what's listening on port 443?'. `netstat -tulpn` is the older version.

questions.q: Restart the nginx service (you have sudo rights).
questions.explain: `systemctl restart nginx`. Other verbs: start, stop, reload, status, enable (start at boot), disable. Use `reload` when the app supports it, to avoid dropping connections.

questions.q: Check whether the SSH daemon (unit name: sshd) is running.
questions.output:
● sshd.service - OpenSSH server daemon
     Loaded: loaded (/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service; enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Sun 2026-11-23 08:01:44 UTC; 1h 30min ago
   Main PID: 801 (sshd)
questions.explain: `systemctl status` shows active state, whether it's enabled at boot, its PID and recent log lines.

questions.q: View the systemd journal logs for ONLY the nginx unit.
questions.output:
Nov 23 09:20:47 netrealm-srv01 nginx[1123]: connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream
Nov 23 09:21:02 netrealm-srv01 systemd[1]: Reloaded nginx.service.
questions.explain: `journalctl -u nginx` filters by unit. Add `-f` to follow, `--since "1 hour ago"` for a time range, `-p err` for errors only.

questions.q: Find the process ID(s) of anything named nginx.
questions.hint: pgrep, or ps piped to grep
questions.explain: `pgrep nginx` prints matching PIDs. The classic is `ps aux | grep nginx`. `pidof` works too.

questions.q: Politely ask process 4021 to terminate (SIGTERM).
questions.explain: `kill PID` sends SIGTERM (15), letting the program clean up. `kill -9` (SIGKILL) can't be caught: use it only as a last resort.

questions.q: Install the curl package on this Ubuntu server.
questions.output:
Reading package lists... Done
The following NEW packages will be installed:
  curl
Setting up curl (8.5.0-2ubuntu10) ...
questions.explain: Debian/Ubuntu: `apt install`. RHEL/Fedora: `dnf install` (older: `yum`). Run `apt update` first to refresh the package index.

questions.q: Change the owner of report.txt to the user alice (you have sudo).
questions.explain: `chown user file` (or `chown user:group file`). Changing ownership normally needs root. Add `-R` for directories.

questions.q: Show free disk space on all mounted filesystems in human-readable units.
questions.output:
Filesystem      Size  Used Avail Use% Mounted on
/dev/sda1        40G   31G  7.2G  82% /
/dev/sdb1       200G   90G  110G  45% /var/lib/docker
questions.explain: `df -h` = disk free per filesystem. `du -sh dir` shows how much space a directory uses.

questions.q: Find every file under /etc whose name ends in .conf.
questions.explain: `find /etc -name "*.conf"`. Quote the pattern so the shell doesn't expand it first. `-type f` limits it to files.

questions.q: Open an SSH session to 10.0.0.5 as the user admin.
questions.output:
admin@10.0.0.5's password:
Welcome to NetRealm Core Router OS
admin@core01:~$
questions.explain: `ssh user@host`. Use key-based auth (`ssh-keygen`, `ssh-copy-id`) instead of passwords where you can.

questions.q: Show just the LAST 20 lines of app.log.
questions.explain: `tail -n 20 file` (or `tail -20`). `head -n 20` gives the first 20 lines.

questions.q: Write the text hello into a NEW file greeting.txt using echo and output redirection (overwrite, don't append).
questions.explain: `>` overwrites (or creates) the file; `>>` appends. `2>` redirects stderr; `&>` redirects both stdout and stderr.

questions.q: What permissions does `chmod 755 script.sh` set?
questions.explain: r=4, w=2, x=1. 7 = rwx (owner), 5 = r-x (group), 5 = r-x (others).

questions.q: What permissions does `chmod 640 secrets.yml` set?
questions.explain: 6 = rw- (owner), 4 = r-- (group), 0 = --- (others). Good for config files with secrets: the owner can edit, the group can read, nobody else sees it.

questions.q: What's the difference between `>` and `>>`?
choices: `>` overwrites the file; `>>` appends to it
questions.explain: `echo hi > f` replaces f's contents; `echo hi >> f` adds a line to the end. Many configs have been destroyed by a single missing `>`!

questions.q: What does the pipe `|` do in `ps aux | grep nginx`?
choices: Sends the stdout of the first command into the stdin of the second
Runs both commands in parallel with no connection
Saves output to a file named grep
Runs the second command only if the first fails
questions.explain: Pipes chain small tools together, the Unix philosophy. `||` (logical OR) runs the second command only if the first fails; `&&` only if it succeeds.

questions.q: What is the UID of the root user?
questions.explain: root is UID 0. Regular users usually start at 1000; 65534 is often 'nobody'.

questions.q: On most modern Linux distributions, what runs as PID 1?
questions.explain: systemd is the init system on most distros: it starts services, adopts orphaned processes and manages units.

questions.q: Which directory holds system-wide configuration files?
questions.explain: /etc = config, /var/log = logs, /home = user files, /bin and /usr/bin = programs, /tmp = temporary files (often wiped at reboot).

questions.q: Where do most traditional log files live?
questions.explain: /var/log holds syslog/messages, auth.log, nginx logs and more. systemd also keeps a binary journal you read with journalctl.

questions.q: What does `sudo` do?
choices: Runs a command with elevated (root) privileges, if you're allowed
Switches to a new shell permanently
questions.explain: sudo = 'superuser do'. Who may use it is controlled by /etc/sudoers (edit with `visudo`). Every use is logged.

questions.q: A command exits with status 0. What does that mean?
questions.explain: 0 = success, anything else = some kind of failure. Check it with `echo $?`. Scripts and CI pipelines rely on this.

questions.q: What is the purpose of `#!/bin/bash` on the first line of a script?
choices: It's the shebang: it tells the OS which interpreter runs the script
It's a comment with no effect
It makes the script run as root
questions.explain: The shebang picks the interpreter. `#!/usr/bin/env python3` is common for Python. The file still needs execute permission.

questions.q: What does `2>&1` do in `./backup.sh > out.log 2>&1`?
choices: Sends stderr (2) to the same place as stdout (1)
questions.explain: File descriptors: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr. This captures errors AND normal output in out.log. Order matters!

questions.q: What does the execute (x) permission mean on a DIRECTORY?
choices: You can enter (cd into) and traverse it
You can run every file inside it
questions.explain: On directories: r = list names, w = create/delete entries, x = enter/traverse. Without x, you can't reach files inside even if you know their names.

questions.q: In bash, what does `$?` contain?
choices: The exit status of the last command
questions.explain: `$?` = last exit code, `$$` = current PID, `$#` = number of arguments, `$1`... = positional arguments, `$@` = all arguments.

questions.q: Which file traditionally lists a Linux host's DNS resolver (nameserver) addresses?
questions.explain: /etc/resolv.conf has `nameserver` lines (often managed by systemd-resolved or NetworkManager). /etc/hosts holds static name-to-IP entries that are checked first.

questions.q: What is /etc/hosts used for?
choices: Static hostname-to-IP mappings checked before DNS
Listing users who can log in
questions.explain: Entries like `10.0.0.5 core01` resolve locally without DNS. Handy for labs, but also a classic source of 'why does only MY machine resolve that wrong?'

questions.q: Which package manager do RHEL, Rocky and Fedora use?
questions.explain: RHEL family: dnf/yum with .rpm packages. Debian/Ubuntu: apt with .deb. Arch: pacman.

questions.q: What does the cron schedule `0 2 * * *` mean?
questions.explain: Fields: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. `0 2 * * *` = minute 0 of hour 2, every day. `*/5 * * * *` = every 5 minutes.

questions.q: What is a zombie process?
choices: A process that has exited but whose parent hasn't collected its exit status
questions.explain: Zombies (<defunct>, state Z) use no CPU, only a process-table slot. They disappear when the parent calls wait() or the parent exits and init reaps them.

questions.q: With `umask 022`, what permissions does a newly created regular file get?
questions.explain: Files start from 666 and directories from 777, then the umask bits are removed: 666 − 022 = 644, 777 − 022 = 755.

questions.q: What octal value represents rwxr-x--- ?
What octal value represents rw-r--r-- ?
questions.explain: rw- = 6, r-- = 4, r-- = 4 → 644. This is the usual mode for regular files.

questions.q: What signal NUMBER is SIGKILL (the one that can't be caught)?
questions.explain: SIGKILL = 9 (`kill -9`), SIGTERM = 15 (the default), SIGHUP = 1 (often 'reload config'), SIGINT = 2 (Ctrl+C).

questions.q: Order the Linux boot sequence.
items: Kernel loads and mounts the root filesystem
questions.explain: Firmware → bootloader → kernel (+ initramfs) → systemd → targets/services → login.

questions.q: Build a pipeline that counts how often each unique 404 line appears, most frequent first. Order the stages.
questions.explain: `uniq` only collapses ADJACENT duplicates, so sort first. Then `uniq -c` counts and `sort -nr` sorts numerically, descending. A classic log-analysis one-liner.

questions.q: Which of these is an ABSOLUTE path?
questions.explain: Absolute paths start at the root `/`. Relative paths start from the current directory (`.` = here, `..` = parent).

questions.q: Which command tests whether TCP port 443 on 10.0.0.5 accepts connections?
questions.explain: `nc -zv host port` (netcat) tries a TCP connect. ping uses ICMP and has no ports! `curl -v https://10.0.0.5` or `telnet 10.0.0.5 443` work too.
